title: The guru
hookLine: Hindu paths give the teacher a weighty place, a relationship to approach with care

lines: WHO TAUGHT YOU TO TIE YOUR SHOES?
HAND TO HAND, NOT BY MANUAL.
cards: Who taught you to tie your shoes? Not a manual. Somebody knelt down, took the laces, went slowly, and let you get it wrong a few times.
Some things travel well in books. Some, it seems, only travel hand to hand, from a person who can do them to a person who wants to.
In the Upanishads, this kind of teaching is pictured that way: handed on by someone who has walked the road, to someone just starting out.
That person has a name, now an English word worn thin by headlines about marketing and fitness.

teach.b: In Sanskrit, guru is a teacher, and as an ordinary adjective it also means heavy, weighty: someone whose words carry weight.

A later text gives a traditional explanation that hears the syllables as darkness and its remover. It's a teaching more than a dictionary entry, but it shows how the role is felt. The Mundaka Upanishad gives the scene.

teach.h: FUEL IN HAND, TO ONE WHO KNOWS AND LIVES IT.
teach.b: A seeker who wants to know what is real should go to a teacher with fuel in hand, a small gift for the teacher's fire.
And it names what to look for: a teacher learned in the sacred texts, and established in Brahman, the ultimate reality.
Two tests, not one. Knowing the texts isn't enough. Living what they point to isn't either.

The Bhagavad Gita adds the student's side. Learn it, Krishna tells Arjuna, by bowing, by asking questions, and by service; the wise who have seen the truth will teach you. Asking questions is right there in the verse.
And the same texts that honor the teacher also warn.

teach.h: THE BLIND LED BY THE BLIND.
teach.b: The Katha Upanishad describes people wise in their own eyes, going round and round, like the blind led by the blind. A guru is trusted with a great deal: a student's time, attention, hopes, sometimes a whole life.
Trust that weighty is the point of the relationship, and it's exactly why it should be given slowly, with eyes open, and with both of the Mundaka's tests in mind.

how: In Hindu traditions that center on a guru, a student seeks out a teacher, often receives instruction or a mantra from them, learns through questions and service, and honors teachers on festivals such as Guru Purnima.

o: a well-known expert on health, money or fitness
a wandering monk who lives by begging alone
a teacher whose words carry weight, in Sanskrit

p: how the seeker comes, in the Mundaka
how the student learns, in the Gita
the blind led by the blind

s: guru only ever meant remover of darkness
as an ordinary adjective it means heavy, weighty. the darkness-remover explanation is a traditional teaching found in a later text.
in the Gita, the student learns by asking questions as well as by service
bowing, asking questions and service: questions are right there in the verse.
the Mundaka asks only that the teacher know the texts
two tests: learned in the sacred texts, and established in Brahman.

games.q: you meet a teacher who is brilliant on stage, but you can't tell whether they live what they teach. by the Mundaka's test, what now?
o: follow them: look how moved everyone is.
look for both: learning, and a life rooted in what's taught.
games.why: the Mundaka names two qualities, learned in the texts and established in Brahman. the texts honor the teacher and still ask for care.

practice: Bring to mind one person who taught you something that mattered, and ask what made their teaching land.
Then picture a teacher for the deepest things you care about, name three qualities you'd look for, and set them beside the Mundaka's two: do they know the tradition, and do they live it?
And one more, from the Gita: would they welcome your questions?

wordCard.voice: Guru. In Sanskrit, a teacher, and weighty: someone whose words carry weight, trusted to hand on what books can't. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: teacher; as an adjective, heavy, weighty.

carryVoice: Your line: choose with care. Yesterday's teacher, Ramana, was such a figure for the people who came to his hill. Back tomorrow, same hill.
